blocks.note: first meaning: in keeping with a nation's founding law
second meaning: a walk taken for the sake of one's health

explanation.surface: Someone asks what measures a careful politician should adopt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Politically correct' is not the modern catchphrase here but a description of lawful government; a constitutional is also an old-fashioned word for a healthy stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: An action permitted by the founding charter is lawful in that sense, and a brisk stroll for health is the noun.

clue.text: Young drinkers may seek desperate remedies

blocks.note: surface reading: children sipping drinks through thin tubes
setter's reading: the idiom for trying any last hope, however feeble

explanation.surface: Children at a party reaching for something to drink with, oddly described as desperate.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom comes from a drowning man grabbing at floating straw; the clue pictures children grabbing the straws in their drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes grasping at any feeble hope or measure when in serious trouble.

clue.text: Rising West Indian company put on Verdi opera

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: someone from Cuba, an island of the West Indies
the usual abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A Caribbean theatre company on the up stages a Verdi work.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'put on' places the company below the reversed islander; the surface makes it sound like staging a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabucco is the Verdi opera about Nebuchadnezzar, famous for its chorus of Hebrew slaves.

blocks.note: first meaning: rapture, an overwhelming feeling of delight
second meaning: conveyance, a means of getting about

explanation.surface: A joyride, the thrill of a stolen car, split into two words.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that 'Joy ride' is to be split into two separate words, each a meaning of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Transports of delight are raptures, and a vehicle that carries you is also called transport.

clue.text: It doesn’t normally contain mother's ruin

definitions.text: It doesn’t normally contain mother's ruin

indicators.note: to ruin something is to wreck it, so the preceding word is broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A flask is usually filled with tea or soup, not with gin.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother's ruin is old British slang for gin. Read cryptically, the same words are the fodder and the anagram signal, while the whole clue describes the flask.
explanation.definitionFit: A vacuum flask is normally filled with hot drinks such as tea or coffee rather than spirits.

blocks.note: surface reading: in the mood to drop in on a neighbour
setter's reading: a local is a British word for one's neighbourhood pub, visited for a drink

explanation.surface: Someone fancies paying a call on somebody nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the local' is the pub nearest home, so wanting a visit there means wanting a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wanting to go to the pub is craving a drink, which is the parched feeling described.

indicators.note: letters moved around are scattered into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Ancient Irish inscriptions found near a town in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Omagh is a town in County Tyrone, Northern Ireland; 'around' looks like location but signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham is the early medieval alphabet of strokes used to write Primitive Irish on standing stones.

definitions.note: the setter uses infers in the looser sense of hints or implies

indicators.note: something incorrect is wrong, so the letters are put in a different order

blocks.note: the total is all of it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone deduces that the sum spent has been miscalculated.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly, a listener infers and a speaker implies; the clue uses 'infers' to mean hints at, which pedants dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: To allude is to refer indirectly or hint, the loose popular sense of inferring something.

clue.text: What those with a walk-on part will do?

definitions.text: What those with a walk-on part will do?

blocks.note: surface reading: a tiny non-speaking role in a play

blocks.clueFragment: What those with a walk-on part will do?
blocks.note: setter's reading: they literally walk on the planks of the stage

explanation.surface: A question about what bit-part actors get up to.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means to act on stage; a walk-on actor walks on the stage floorboards literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to perform as an actor in the theatre, the stage being made of planks.

blocks.note: first meaning: an old literary word for shadow or shelter from sun
second meaning: offence taken, as in taking it

explanation.surface: A hint or slight trace of resentment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shade of' reads as 'a slight amount of'; in fact shade is one meaning, from Latin umbra, shadow.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Latin for shadow and survives mainly in the phrase about taking offence.

clue.text: Rough long-haired dog taken out - for a breather?

definitions.note: the inhaler is the device a breather uses

indicators.note: something taken out is removed, so its letters are struck from the longer word
rough means disordered, so the remaining letters are shuffled

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen dropped
taken as written; these three letters are removed

explanation.surface: A shaggy dog is taken outside for a breath of air.
explanation.walkthrough: Take D, O and G out of LONGHAIRED and rearrange what is left. 'Breather' suggests a short rest, but here it is someone breathing.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthmatics and other people with breathing trouble use a puffer device to take medicine into the lungs.

clue.text: They may be game to take the helm, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the answer is a word pronounced like the phrase

blocks.note: to cox is to steer a rowing boat

explanation.surface: Some people may be willing to take charge of steering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like willing, but means game birds: cock pheasants and gamecocks. A cox steers a rowing eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Male birds such as pheasants and fighting gamecocks are game, hunted or set to fight.

blocks.note: a Mass is a church service
media are vehicles of expression, plural of medium

explanation.surface: Vans and trucks used by maintenance or delivery crews.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: newspapers and broadcasters are channels that serve the public with news.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers, radio and television are channels serving a wide public with news and entertainment.

clue.text: So Lou and Mary got together in a loving way

indicators.note: things that get together mingle, so the named letters are mixed into one new word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people named Lou and Mary became a couple, tenderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So' looks like a connective but its letters belong in the mix with both names.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb for acting with romantic affection or desire, from the Latin word for love.

clue.text: Not flush, but accepted by the social clique

blocks.note: if you are accepted by a group, you are in
a set is a social circle, as in the jet set

explanation.surface: Someone short of money is nonetheless welcomed by the fashionable crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flush' suggests having plenty of cash; here it means level with a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A panel set back into a surface rather than level with it is recessed, so not flush.

clue.text: Having private information? No, we think otherwise

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the letters are taken in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone denies holding inside knowledge, and others disagree.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone privy to secret or insider facts is well informed, the meaning of the idiom.

definitions.note: a place found in that country

blocks.note: first meaning: a division or rift
second meaning: a port on the Dalmatian coast, now in Croatia

explanation.surface: The breakup of a Balkan federation in the 1990s.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a general comment on the Balkan wars; the second meaning is a specific Adriatic city.
explanation.definitionFit: A rift between factions is a division, and the Croatian port is a city of the former Yugoslav state.

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pipe joint that drips badly.
explanation.definitionFit: A link or joining between two things or parts is a connection, as in mechanical coupling.

blocks.note: surface reading: the first woman, made as Adam's companion
setter's reading: aboard ship, the officer ranking next below the captain

explanation.surface: The biblical first woman cast adrift or confused.
explanation.walkthrough: Eve was Adam's first partner; on a merchant ship the same title belongs to the second-in-command. 'At sea' could mean bewildered, but it means on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Eve was the original wife, and on a merchant vessel the chief officer below the captain holds this title.

clue.text: Possibly slip up providing Spanish and German articles

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the next word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: providing means on condition that
el is the Spanish word for the
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: Someone might make a mistake when supplying foreign grammar words.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, slip is a fielding position beside the wicketkeeper. 'Slip up' looks like one phrase, but the clue splits it.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip is a cricket close-catching position, so the player stationed there is one example of a fieldsman.

blocks.note: a roll is a small loaf of bread
to sup is to sip or drink

explanation.surface: Someone turns up bringing food and refreshments.
explanation.walkthrough: Sup is an old-fashioned verb for taking liquid in small mouthfuls; the obvious break after the S is the wrong one.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrasal verb means to turn up somewhere, often casually or late.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who turns labour into fun
setter's reading: someone who turns a literary work such as a novel into a stage play

explanation.surface: A cheerful person who turns chores into games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' and 'play' look like opposites, but 'work' is a book and 'play' a drama; 'perhaps' warns that a play is one kind of version.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer who reworks a novel for the stage or screen is producing a version of the original.

clue.text: Remind one that it's time for church?

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for stirring a memory
second meaning: literally sound a chime to call worshippers

explanation.surface: Prompting someone that the Sunday service is about to start.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to seem familiar or jog memory, and a church summons worshippers by chiming.

blocks.note: surface reading: something more than twelve inches long
setter's reading: the joint located directly above the foot

explanation.surface: Describing something measuring more than twelve inches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over a foot' reads as a length; it is a position on the leg.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint linking the leg to the foot sits just above it, so it is literally over the foot.

blocks.note: an era is a period of time
taken as written

explanation.surface: A moment arrives for quiet reflection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muse' looks like a verb meaning ponder, but it is a noun: one of the nine Greek goddesses.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is one of the nine Greek goddesses of the arts, presiding over love poetry.

blocks.note: first meaning: struck hard
second meaning: informal for worn out

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster worn out after punishing pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: Hit with a sharp blow is the literal sense, and very tired is a colloquial sense of the same word.

clue.text: Spaniard at the centre is a politician

indicators.note: putting something at the centre places it inside the middle of the other word

blocks.note: señor is the Spanish title for a man
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Spanish man at the heart of things turns out to be in government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the centre' looks like one phrase meaning central; split it, so 'at' goes into the centre of the Spaniard.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of an upper legislative chamber, such as the US Senate, is an elected politician.

clue.text: They stretch from pole to pole

definitions.text: They stretch from pole to pole

blocks.note: surface reading: from the North Pole to the South Pole, right across the globe

blocks.clueFragment: They stretch from pole to pole
blocks.note: setter's reading: cables strung between wooden posts along a road

explanation.surface: Something spanning the whole Earth, from Arctic to Antarctic.
explanation.walkthrough: The poles sound geographic; they are wooden posts carrying cables.
explanation.definitionFit: Old message cables were strung overhead between tall wooden posts along roads and railways.
